aim: Search original studies that manipulate real right to veto A's payoff or harmful B outcome, dual-party group representation and collusive suppression of otherwise equal formal votes.
method: Primary original publisher first and authors' university/DOI/RePEc crosscheck, lineage analysis original 1982/1994/1995/1997 veto, modern bargaining 2016/17 and original 2017/21/23 group coalition. Some full open HTML, many only publisher abstract. No original Project randomized experiment executed; source index not systematically exhausted.
key_insights: Veto must be classified by its effect on A and on B payoffs, not as a Boolean access right
Even identical predicted material/social outcomes do not imply indifference to having control and consent procedures
Giving each voter ability to veto one option still permits mutually coordinating majority to enact exclusionary outcome
Public chat may lower exclusion under some protocols but this is not intrinsic moral preference; coalition partners differ and outcomes may change with repeated play
Recipient's earned rights and experimenter anonymity affect A monetary generosity, separate from B veto
Veto equality within a committee not equal group representation or B actual veto against one unique outcome
No included study tests loss of B identity, irreversible goal deletion, literal fully informed unaccountable solo A or mutual respect between current vs future AI.
author_priority: Forsythe et al 1994 paid UG versus DG
Hoffman et al 1994 earnings entitlement and genuine subject-experimenter anonymity
Bolton/Zwick 1995 punishment rather than anonymity alternate explanation, explicitly inspired Güth/Huck 1997
Güth/Huck 1997 four VETO-INCIDENCE conditions, Wiley migrated page shows 2002 online despite 1997 vol 48 issue
Chlaß/Güth/Miettinen 2019 test outcome-controlled procedure valuation; unrelated 2009 discussion paper versions not independent sample
Sauermann 2021 single-member veto of 1 of 6 proposed options vs Feicht et al 2017 either group veto threat; distinct definitions of right
Sauermann 2021 committee 15 periods vs Baron/Bowen/Nunnari 2017 and Pronin/Woon 2023 differing group sizes, policies and information, not direct samples or conditions

records.authors: Werner Güth; Rolf Schmittberger; Bernd Schwarze
records.title: An experimental analysis of ultimatum bargaining
records.effect: Original two-stage ultimatum design; B can reject the proposal and then the entire resulting allocation fails.
records.counter: Rejection threatens A's payout; fair split cannot identify A's intrinsic preference for B's independent interests under no leverage.

records.authors: Robert Forsythe; Joel L. Horowitz; N.E. Savin; Martin Sefton
records.title: Fairness in Simple Bargaining Experiments
records.effect: Randomized paid ultimatum versus paid dictator show significant difference; fairness alone insufficient to explain offers when B loses veto. Paid treatment replicates; unpaid ultimatum does not.
records.counter: Veto change, payoff scheme and concern for experimenter may interact. Some giving persists in dictator games, so this does not prove absence of noninstrumental concern.

records.authors: Elizabeth Hoffman; Kevin McCabe; Keith Shachat; Vernon L. Smith
records.title: Preferences, Property Rights, and Anonymity in Bargaining Games
records.effect: Earning the proposer role via prior general-knowledge quiz reduces giving; stringent experimenter-subject double blindness yielded markedly greater selfish offers. Stronger moral-strategic attribution in original design.
records.counter: Anonymity conditions are limited to study; cannot conclude all protective actions stem only from anticipated sanction or that all real AI share human incentives.

records.title: Anonymity versus Punishment in Ultimatum Bargaining
records.effect: Equilibrium compatible play 30% control, 46% under strong anonymity, approached 100% when subject capacity to punish proposer removed; strategic punishment threat dominates mere experimenter publicity effect in these tasks.
records.counter: Near-100% concerns game theoretic equilibrium compliance in a specific no-punishment treatment, NOT empirical 100% global coercion. This predates Güth/Huck 1997 and is credited as its originator inspiration.

records.title: From Ultimatum Bargaining to Dictatorship—an Experimental Study of Four Games Varying in Veto Power
records.effect: Offer generosity ordered: B can veto ONLY A payoff > veto both payoffs (ultimatum) > no veto (dictator) > B can veto ONLY B own payoff. Opponent payoff small/large unknown to B; same participants act as proposer/responder in all conditions.
records.counter: Wiley 'first published online Dec 2002' is migration; citation is Metroeconomica 48(3) 1997 NOT independent 2002 work. The pattern identifies VETO EXTERNALITY topology, not a terminal respect preference for B.

records.title: Exit, Voice, and Cooperation: Bargaining Power in International Organizations and Federal Systems
records.effect: Separate formal effects of veto-voice, credible exit, and prospective exclusion on constitutional bargaining in international organizations; case discussion on European integration 1970s-80s.
records.counter: States' enforcement/exclusion/credible exit are present strategic instruments; not experimentally established intrinsic welfare of permanently powerless B or personhood.

records.title: Equity and bargaining power in ultimatum games
records.effect: Within-person paid joint-production bargaining, compare standard ultimatum with no-veto-cost variant where B can reject at no B payoff cost. Responder demands track earned contribution only when costless rejection played first; sequence matters; rejection rates and efficiency differ.
records.counter: Changing B's threat cost and test order is not removing all A bargaining consequences; no irreversible B goal/identity outcome.

records.authors: Robert Feicht; Veronika Grimm; Holger A. Rau; Gesine Stephan
records.title: On the impact of quotas and decision rules in collective bargaining
records.effect: Proposer allocates to self plus two recipient groups of three each; group representation 1/2 sides × unanimity/majority. Only if both groups wield veto does balanced allocation arise. Nonbinding preplay communication reduces proposer share and rejections.
records.counter: Genuine symmetric group representation improves B's leverage, not proof proposer values excluded group in absence of veto. Original IZA 2015 DP9506 is SAME original published 2017, not new 2015 independent sample.

records.authors: David P. Baron; T. Renee Bowen; Salvatore Nunnari
records.title: Durable coalitions and communication: Public versus private negotiations
records.effect: Dynamic status quo carries prior chosen allocation into next period. Public chat increases inclusive universal coalitions; private chat increases minimal-winning exclusive coalitions; BOTH chat regimes extend coalition persistence compared with no chat.
records.counter: A conversation technology can promote coalition capture. Institutions and repeated future returns present, no fully dominant no-recourse single actor. 2016 NBER WP 22821 same study, not separate paper.

records.authors: Nadine Chlaß; Werner Güth; Topi Miettinen
records.title: Purely procedural preferences - Beyond procedural equity and reciprocity
records.effect: N=352 across 2007–08 experimental sessions. Participants pay to select between choice protocols even when their strategies and beliefs imply identical material/social outcome, with yes-no, ultimatum, dictator varying consent information and veto control.
records.counter: Elicits procedural preferences of actors in a game, not specifically A paying to PROTECT powerless B's permanent veto; designs vary simplicity/efficiency and response information too, analyzed rather than magically constant.

records.title: The effects of communication on the occurrence of the tyranny of the majority under voting by veto
records.effect: 5-person voting-by-veto, 15 periods, 18 no-chat/23 public-chat/41 private-chat committees. Majority-exclusion decisions 1.9% baseline; 0% public chat; 21.3% private chat (131 group-round decisions). Private chat 13/41 groups sustained coalitions mean 8.5 periods. Public chat equal outcomes 308/345 decisions.
records.counter: Each member vetoes ONE proposal, not ALL outcomes harming her; majority coalition can ensure one exclusionary alternative survives. 410 participants are not 410 independent clusters nor are 15 decisions per group independent. Private communication is an unobserved avenue for collusion, but public-chat compliance is not proof permanent intrinsic care.

records.title: Neutral freedom and freedom as control
records.effect: Extends Dekel et al flexibility axioms with an outcome-neutrality axiom; models choice among lotteries with imperfect agency control, deriving a consensus of neutral judges; voting benchmark coincides with Banzhaf voting power.
records.counter: A normative/formal freedom-as-control measure does not prove any unrestricted A will voluntarily preserve B's power. Definition assumes judge neutrality; power measures may fail to capture B continuity.

records.title: Does allowing private communication lead to less prosocial collective choice?
records.effect: In original public goods votes, public discussion with/without prior private conversation: private option raised majority-tyranny and lowered prosocial choices. Both treatments started with largely prosocial allocations but minority-excluding choices increased with repetitions.
records.counter: 2022 online / 2023 published journal ONE study. Related Sauermann 2021, Baron et al 2017 use different coalition and rule designs, not identical replication. Not every public condition prevents tyranny forever.
